meta.description: Not George Herbert. The earliest known printing is an 1891 Oakland quotation book that credits P. T. Barnum with no source. Herbert wrote a different line.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If I Shoot at the Sun, I May Hit a Star'?
meta.ogDescription: Herbert never wrote it. The oldest known copy is an 1891 quotation book crediting P. T. Barnum, with no source given. Quote Investigator found no Barnum text.

answer.label: Not George Herbert — first credited to P. T. Barnum
answer.sourceLine: Herbert supplied the thought, not the sentence. Quote Investigator ↗ calls his 1633 verse — “who aimeth at the sky, / Shoots higher much then he that means a tree” — “an important aboriginal source” for this whole family of sayings, but the sun-and-star wording appears nowhere in his work. Its earliest known printing is an 1891 quotation book compiled by an Oakland church society, where it sits under P. T. Barnum’s name with no source attached — and Quote Investigator found no Barnum book or interview containing it.

source.heading: The oldest known printing of this wording

docMeta.dd: Comp. Ladies of the First Unitarian Church of Oakland, California. San Francisco: C. A. Murdock & Co., 1891 — page 24.
“P. T. Barnum” — a bare name, with no book, date or page given.
“The Church-porch,” in The Temple (1633) — a different sentence, about the sky and a tree.

source.excerpt:
Jealousy is a secret avowal of inferiority.
— Massillon.

If I shoot at the sun, I may hit a star.
— P. T. Barnum.

The world is a school, and the business of its occupants, the pursuit of an education fitting them to graduate into the invisible university of God.
— W. R. Alger.
trail: 1633 — the verse the whole family grew from. Herbert’s “The Church-porch,” the opening poem of The Temple, reads: “Sink not in spirit. Who aimeth at the sky, / Shoots higher much then he that means a tree.” A sky and a tree — no sun and no star in the verse. Neither “shoot at the sun” nor “hit a star” occurs anywhere in the poem. Read it at Wikisource ↗

1846 and 1879 — what Victorians actually put in Herbert’s mouth. Quote Investigator finds his name attached twice, and both times to a moon version: “we had better shoot at the moon if we want to hit a high mark” (The English Review, December 1846) and “that it is good to shoot at the moon even though you only hit a tree” (1879). Neither is the sun-and-star sentence. See QI’s citation list ↗

1891 — the wording surfaces, already unsourced. On page 24 of More Borrowings, compiled by the Ladies of the First Unitarian Church of Oakland, California, the sentence appears under the name “P. T. Barnum” and no other information. It is the earliest instance Quote Investigator could find, and it appeared in the year Barnum died. Read the scan ↗

The compilers have form. The companion volume by the same Oakland church society, Borrowings (1889), was for many years the earliest known source of Emerson’s “better mousetrap” line. Compiler Sarah S. B. Yule later explained the method herself: she had copied words “from an address delivered long years ago” into a private handbook, and “when we were compiling ‘Borrowings’ I drew from this old handbook freely.” Quote Investigator on the mousetrap ↗
source.excerptNote: How the line actually appears — one entry in an unsourced anthology. Every item in the volume carries a name and nothing else, and the book’s own index confirms the page: “Barnum, P. T., 24.”

source.rightsNote: Both the sentence and the verse behind it are long out of copyright in the United States. More Borrowings — the volume carrying the earliest known printing of this wording — was published in San Francisco in 1891, decades before the 1931 threshold, and the Internet Archive’s scan is marked not in copyright. George Herbert’s The Temple dates to 1633.

author.name: George Herbert
author.heading: George Herbert wrote the verse, not the proverb
author.metaLine: 1593–1633 · English poet, orator and Anglican priest
author.bio: George Herbert (3 April 1593 – 1 March 1633) was an English poet, orator and priest of the Church of England, and the quietest of the metaphysical poets. Shortly before he died he sent the manuscript of his English poems to his friend Nicholas Ferrar, who published them in 1633 as The Temple: Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations; its opening poem, “The Church-porch,” carries the aim-high stanza that everything here descends from. Herbert was also a working collector of proverbs — his Outlandish Proverbs (1640) gathered over a thousand sayings from many countries — and that, more than anything he actually wrote, is why anonymous folk wisdom keeps drifting onto his name.

misattribution.heading: Three credits, no origin
misattribution.intro: This is a proverb that has been handed from name to name for nearly two centuries, rearranging its own scenery as it goes. Three credits circulate for it, and not one of them is documented as the source of this wording.

items.tag: the credit on most quote pages
items.why: Herbert did write a genuinely related verse in 1633, and Quote Investigator calls it “an important aboriginal source” for the whole class of sayings. But it is a different sentence: “who aimeth at the sky, / Shoots higher much then he that means a tree.” The words “shoot at the sun” and “hit a star” appear nowhere in “The Church-porch” ↗, and Herbert’s own Outlandish Proverbs ↗ contains no proverb mentioning a star at all.

The 1891 anthology is the first known appearance of the sentence and it does print his name — but after searching, Quote Investigator reports ↗ it “was unable to find direct evidence, i.e., a book by Barnum or an interview containing the statement.” The credit surfaced in 1891, the year Barnum died, in a small church-society giftbook that sourced nothing it printed. The line is absent from Wikiquote’s Barnum page ↗ entirely.

items.who: Norman Vincent Peale, W. Clement Stone and Les Brown
items.why: The version most people meet today — “Shoot for the moon. Even if you miss, you’ll land among the stars” — is a twentieth-century descendant of the same proverb, not an original. Quote Investigator dates it to Peale in 1988, to W. Clement Stone in a 1996 Usenet post and to Les Brown in 2000, with Britney Spears offering her own version the same year. QI tracks all of them ↗

misattribution.truthLine: It is a proverb, not a quotation. Its oldest known printing is page 24 of More Borrowings (1891) ↗, where it sits under P. T. Barnum’s name with no source — and nobody has yet found it in anything Barnum, or Herbert, actually wrote.

context.heading: A proverb that keeps rearranging its own sky
lead: The saying has been swapping its props for two centuries, and Quote Investigator’s chronology shows how freely. Shoot at the moon and hit the top of the highest tree, said an 1859 novel — already calling it “the old saying.” Shoot at the stars and you may hit a tree, said the Saturday Review in 1865. Shoot an arrow at the sun every morning, a Michigan paper reported a speaker at an 1876 pioneers’ reunion urging, and when told the sun could not be hit he answered: “You will hit higher than if you aimed lower.” By 1904 a Cleveland paper was running the form as a joke: “Aim at a chorus girl,” and you may hit a star.

Astronomy is the part that never settles, because astronomy was never the point. What survives intact from Herbert’s 1633 stanza is the argument underneath — aim high and you will overshoot whatever you would have reached by aiming low. The celestial furniture is decoration, and it is the decoration, rather than the thought, that keeps being reattributed to whoever is most famous at the time.
detailsBody: 1633 — George Herbert, “The Church-porch”: aim at the sky, not at a tree.
1846 — The English Review credits Herbert with a moon version: “we had better shoot at the moon if we want to hit a high mark.”
1859 — already “the old saying”: “Shoot at the moon and you will hit the top of the highest tree.”
1876 — the sun enters, as the target for a daily arrow.
1891 — the sun-and-star wording appears in print for the first time, under P. T. Barnum’s name, in More Borrowings.
1914 — a Michigan bakery uses “P. T. Barnum said…” to sell Harvest Bread.
1941 — Jane Russell gives an Associated Press interviewer the moon version: “If we aim at the moon—we may hit a star!”
1988–2000 — the moon-and-stars rewrite is used or credited in turn by Norman Vincent Peale, W. Clement Stone, Britney Spears and Les Brown.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI's earliest known instance of "If I shoot at the sun, I may hit a star" is an 1891 collection ascribed to P. T. Barnum, and QI "was unable to find direct evidence, i.e., a book by Barnum or an interview containing the statement."

QI states Herbert's 1633 "Church-Porch" verse was "an important aboriginal source," and quotes the stanza "Pitch thy behaviour low, thy projects high; ... who aimeth at the sky, / Shoots higher much, than he that means a tree."

QI documents Herbert's name attached to moon versions in 1846 (The English Review: "we had better shoot at the moon if we want to hit a high mark") and 1879 ("that it is good to shoot at the moon even though you only hit a tree").

QI documents the 1859 "old saying" (moon / top of the highest tree), the 1865 Saturday Review stars-and-tree line, the 1876 "shoot an arrow at the sun every morning ... You will hit higher than if you aimed lower," and the 1904 Cleveland Leader parody "Aim at a chorus girl," and you may hit a star."
QI documents the 1914 Muskegon Chronicle Harvest Bread advertisement quoting "P. T. Barnum said, 'If I shoot at the sun, I may hit a star.'"

QI documents the 1941 Jane Russell AP interview ("If we aim at the moon—we may hit a star!"), Norman Vincent Peale in 1988 ("Shoot for the moon. If you miss it, you will still land among the stars."), W. Clement Stone in a 1996 Usenet post, Britney Spears in 2000 and Les Brown in 2000.

QI's bibliographic note 7 cites the 1891 source as: More Borrowings, Compiled by Ladies of the First Unitarian Church of Oakland, California, Quote Page 24, C. A. Murdock & Co., Printers, San Francisco, California.
QI's George Herbert category page lists the article "If I Shoot at the Sun, I May Hit a Star," confirming Herbert is one of the names QI examined for this saying.

The Internet Archive scan of More Borrowings (San Francisco: C. A. Murdock & Co., 1891; copyright 1891 by Sarah S. B. Yule and Mary S. Keene) contains, on page 24, "If I shoot at the sun, I may hit a star. — P. T. Barnum" between entries credited to Massillon and W. R. Alger; the book's index reads "Barnum, P. T., 24." Verified in the item's own OCR text (moreborrowings00ladi_djvu.txt). The item is marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT.

Wikisource's text of "The Church-porch" from The Temple (1633) contains the stanza "Pitch thy behaviour low, thy projects high; / So shalt thou humble and magnanimous be: / Sink not in spirit. Who aimeth at the sky, / Shoots higher much then he that means a tree..." and neither "shoot at the sun" nor "hit a star" appears anywhere in the poem.

A full-text scan of The Poems of George Herbert contains the "aimeth at the sky" stanza and returns zero occurrences of "shoot at the sun," "hit a star" or "shoot at the moon" across the whole volume.
CCEL's transcription of Herbert's Outlandish Proverbs (with translations) contains zero occurrences of the word "star," and none of "shoot at the sun," "hit a star" or "shoot at the moon."

Wikiquote's George Herbert page contains no instance of "shoot at the sun," "hit a star," "aimeth at the sky" or "Shoots higher much" in any section, and gives Herbert's life dates as 3 April 1593 – 1 March 1633, describing him as an English poet, orator and priest of the Church of England.
Wikiquote's P. T. Barnum page does not contain "If I shoot at the sun, I may hit a star" anywhere, and gives his dates as 5 July 1810 – 7 April 1891.

QI's mousetrap article states that Borrowings (1889), "gathered by the 'Ladies of the First Unitarian Church of Oakland, California'," was for many years the earliest known match for Emerson's mousetrap saying, and quotes compiler Sarah S. B. Yule: "I copied it in my handbook from an address delivered long years ago ... and when we were compiling 'Borrowings' I drew from this old handbook freely."

George Herbert (3 April 1593 – 1 March 1633) was an English poet, orator and priest of the Church of England; shortly before his death he sent his manuscript to Nicholas Ferrar, and in 1633 his English poems were published as The Temple: Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations, beginning with "The Church Porch."
Herbert compiled Outlandish Proverbs (1640), containing "over 1000 aphorisms in English, but gathered from many countries," reissued in 1651 as Jacula Prudentum.
AZQuotes credits "If I shoot at the sun, I may hit a star" to P. T. Barnum with no source, book or date given — an example of the undocumented credit in circulation.
